extracted.intended_audience: attorneys who practice before the USPTO (respondents, disciplinary counsel), and persons interested in USPTO attorney-discipline procedures
extracted.subtask_description: An initial decision in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding applying the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and related federal statutes/regulations to allegations of attorney misconduct (neglect, failure to inform client, dishonesty, etc.), and determining liability and sanctions. The document explains procedural burdens, statute-of-limitations rules, evidentiary standards, aggravating/mitigating factors, and appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; thereafter the Respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.49. This standard governs how the trier of fact assesses the evidence and allocates the burden between the prosecution (OED Director) and the respondent on affirmative defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for USPTO discipline (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proceeding shall be commenced not later than the earlier of (a) 10 years after the date on which the misconduct forming the basis for the proceeding occurred, or (b) 1 year after the date on which the misconduct is made known to an officer or employee of the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act amended limitations for USPTO matters; cases that lapsed before the AIA remain governed by prior law (e.g., 28 U.S.C. § 2462). Provides application timing examples and notes that the amended statute applies to cases not already lapsed as of AIA enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing violations doctrine (when to toll limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts apply the continuing-violation doctrine only if (1) explicit statutory or regulatory language defines the violation as continuous, or (2) the nature of the offense is such that Congress/agency must have intended it to be continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a strong presumption against treating offenses as continuing. The decision applies this test to 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8) (failure to inform client) and finds that the duty to inform is continuing because it remains active until the client is informed or representation ends; thus tolling may apply in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and standards for 'neglect' (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.' Neglect is defined as omission of proper attention (inadvertent, negligent, or willful) and, per ABA opinion, involves indifference and consistent failure to carry out obligations rather than a single inadvertent error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect generally requires a pattern or course of conduct and a time element; single honest mistakes normally do not constitute neglect, though a single negligent act can be neglect if it causes serious harm (example: failing to appear at a hearing leading to dismissal). Cites Black's Law Dictionary and ABA Informal Opinion 1273; gives examples and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of significant correspondence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform clients of significant correspondence from the PTO; failure to do so is proscribed and may constitute a continuing violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates adequacy of communications (e.g., whether an email included a copy of the Office Action, accurate description of rejections, applicable reply periods). An email omitting key facts or copies can be deficient. The duty continues until the practitioner informs the client or ceases representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to client inquiries and explain matters (communication standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys are required to respond to clients' reasonable requests for information and explain matters sufficiently to allow informed decisions (analogous to Florida Bar Rules 4-1.4(a),(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated failure to answer urgent emails/phone calls or to explain status is problematic and can be aggravating. The decision treats prolonged nonresponse (multiple messages over months/years) as evidence of neglect and grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to deliver client funds/property and render accounting (analogous to Florida Bar Rule 4-1.15(b) / 37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must promptly deliver to a client funds or property to which the client is entitled and render a full accounting of charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to return unearned fees or client property is sanctionable and is relied upon as an aggravating factor. The decision draws parallels between state bar rules and PTO disciplinary rules in evaluating such conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docketing, case-monitoring, and PAIR/customer-number expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to monitor application status (e.g., use PAIR by associating customer number), respond to examiner calls, and maintain an effective docketing system to track deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although use of PAIR is not mandatory, it is strongly encouraged to avoid missed communications. Reliance solely on physical mail, infrequent tickler checks, or a minimalistic docket system that misses deadlines can constitute neglect. The decision critiques six-month tickler checks and failure to follow up on examiner voice messages as inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and qualification of expert testimony in disciplinary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony is allowed only if 'scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will assist the hearing officer to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue.' Experts must be disclosed and provide written reports as required by the Notice of Hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of an expert deposition transcript from a prior malpractice proceeding without qualifying the witness, disclosing the expert, or providing a report violates procedures and risks excluding the evidence as more prejudicial than probative. A party should subpoena the expert to testify if they want the court to consider that testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural compliance and evidence admissibility (probative vs. prejudicial balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence not submitted in accordance with procedural rules (e.g., lacking proper disclosures, failing to qualify witnesses) may be excluded if its admission would be prejudicial or would allow a party to sidestep rules that assure fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court sustained objections to transcripts and exhibits where the offering party failed to follow disclosure/expert rules or where admission would disadvantage the opposing party who had no opportunity to cross-examine. Court balances minimal probative value against prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on scandalous or indecent statements in filings (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from making scandalous or indecent statements in papers filed in the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing incendiary, unsupported, or potentially libelous comments in briefs or filings can itself be a violation and an aggravating factor when assessing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and factors for imposing sanctions (ABA Standards and 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions are determined by weighing aggravating and mitigating factors per the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and considering factors in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision lists aggravating factors (e.g., prior offenses; dishonest/selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; bad faith obstruction; submission of false evidence; refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature; victim vulnerability; substantial experience; indifference to restitution; illegal conduct) and mitigating factors (e.g., no prior offenses; no dishonest motive; personal problems; good-faith effort to make restitution; full disclosure/cooperation; inexperience; character/reputation; physical/mental disability; delay in proceedings; imposition of other sanctions; remorse; remoteness). The court balances these to select appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (examples used to increase sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific aggravating factors include: prior disciplinary offenses; dishonest or selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; bad-faith obstruction of proceedings; submission of false evidence or statements; refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing; victim vulnerability; substantial legal experience; indifference to restitution; illegal conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of multiple aggravating factors, particularly prior similar discipline and obstruction of investigations, supports harsher sanctions (e.g., longer suspension). The decision identifies six aggravating factors present in the respondent's record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (examples used to reduce sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical mitigating factors include: absence of prior offenses; absence of dishonest motive; personal or emotional problems; timely good-faith effort to make restitution; full and free disclosure/cooperation; inexperience; good character/reputation; physical or mental disability or chemical dependency; delay in proceedings; imposition of other sanctions; remorse; remoteness of prior offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court found two mitigating factors in the record (distracting personal matters and lack of dishonest motive) but treated them as less impactful than the aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing malpractice standard of care from disciplinary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of care in a malpractice case is not necessarily relevant to an attorney-discipline proceeding, and a malpractice expert's testimony or report from prior litigation may not satisfy procedural and relevance requirements in a discipline hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court found prior malpractice expert deposition of only minimal value, and it was excluded because it was not offered according to expert disclosure procedures and the OED Director had not had the opportunity to cross-examine the expert in this proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of continuing-impact vs continuing-violation reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory tolling for limitations is based on when the violation ends (for continuing violations), not when the impact of the violation ends; continuing-impact theories do not necessarily extend the statute of limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explains that for failure-to-inform rules (which are continuing), the clock starts when the practitioner actually informs the client (or ceases representation), not when the harm from non-disclosure manifests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for withdrawal/termination of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who ceases to represent a client should take formal steps (e.g., file notice of withdrawal, revoke power of attorney) and return client files/property; failing to file a notice of withdrawal or revoke a power of attorney may be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining power of attorney after effectively ceasing communication or retaining client files can feed into findings of neglect or failure to deliver client property and may be an aggravating fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning options and reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director (and hearing judge) may suspend or exclude a person from practice under 35 U.S.C. § 32 for incompetence, gross misconduct, or violation of USPTO regulations; sanctions should reflect aggravation/mitigation and may include suspension duration and conditions such as passing the MPRE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision imposed an eight-month suspension and required passing the MPRE before reinstatement; cites 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.54(b), 11.58 (duties while suspended), and 11.60(c) (reinstatement). Non-dishonest violations militate against maximum sanctions; prior discipline and obstruction can increase sanction severity.
